articles.excerpt: AI answers are now the first place buyers meet your brand. ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Google AI Overviews all have an opinion about your product — and they cite sources. The problem: there's no UI t…
articles.body: AI answers are now the first place buyers meet your brand. ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Google AI Overviews all have an opinion about your product — and they cite sources. The problem: there's no UI to query them programmatically at scale. This post shows the pattern I use to pull those answers as JSON so you can diff them over time. The shape of the problem Every engine answers differently: ChatGPT gives a synthesized answer plus cited sources and (in search mode) the fan-out queries it ran Gemini returns an answer with grounding links Copilot cites Bing results Google AI Overviews / AI Mode return answer text plus ranked source positions What you actually want as a developer is one normalized object: { answer, sources[], rank, country } per engine.

articles.title: Converting Images Entirely in the Browser: No Uploads Needed
articles.excerpt: Most "free online image converters" work the same way: you upload a file, a server processes it, and you download the result. That's fine until the image is a passport scan, a client mockup, or a pers…
articles.body: Most "free online image converters" work the same way: you upload a file, a server processes it, and you download the result. That's fine until the image is a passport scan, a client mockup, or a personal photo you'd rather not send to an unknown server. Modern browsers can do this work locally. Here's how the client-side approach works. Decoding and re-encoding with the Canvas API The core loop is simple: Read the file with createImageBitmap(file) (or a FileReader ). Draw it onto a <canvas> (or an OffscreenCanvas in a worker). Export with canvas.toBlob(callback, 'image/webp', 0.8) . toBlob handles format conversion (PNG, JPEG, WebP, and AVIF where the browser supports encoding it), and the quality argument gives you lossy compression for free.

articles.title: Syncing level data from seven games into a static Next.js site
articles.excerpt: Mobile Casual Games is a guide hub for puzzle games. It currently covers seven of them, and the level rows behind those guides add up to just over 8,000. New walkthroughs keep landing in the database,…
articles.body: Mobile Casual Games is a guide hub for puzzle games. It currently covers seven of them, and the level rows behind those guides add up to just over 8,000. New walkthroughs keep landing in the database, so the data moves constantly. The site itself is an output: "export" Next.js build: no runtime API, no database connection, nothing fetched when a visitor loads a page. Every level list, every range page, every redirect was decided at build time from JSON files that live in the repository. That raises a practical question: when the data keeps changing, how does it get from wherever it was produced into a static bundle without anything breaking in between? This is how the pipeline works. Where the rows come from The source of truth is a Neon Postgres database with two tables.

articles.body: Documenting Urban Life Through a Documentary Lens The October wind carried a sharp chill through the avenue, scattering golden leaves across damp pavements. As an urban documentary photographer, autumn has always been my favorite season to observe the city. People move with a distinct rhythm, bundled in heavy coats, lost in their thoughts while navigating the shifting weather. That afternoon, a broadcast regarding upcoming municipal urban updates had just concluded across local stations. After what they had heard, a mixed atmosphere reigned on the streets in mid-fall. Some pedestrians hurried past without looking up, eager to reach the warmth of nearby cafes, while small groups lingered by street corners, exchanging quiet impressions and debating the details.

articles.title: AGND, DGND and Chassis Ground: The Three Grounding Questions Everyone Asks
articles.excerpt: Grounding advice has a reputation for contradicting itself. Split the plane; don't split the plane. Ground the chassis; don't make loops. Part of the problem is that three different questions get aske…
articles.body: Grounding advice has a reputation for contradicting itself. Split the plane; don't split the plane. Ground the chassis; don't make loops. Part of the problem is that three different questions get asked as if they were one. They have different answers, and knowing which one you're facing is most of the job. 1. The chip has AGND and DGND pins. Do I connect them? ADCs, DACs and some sensors have separate AGND and DGND pins, and the names make it sound like an instruction to keep two grounds apart. It isn't. The pins are separate inside the package so the analog and digital currents don't share the chip's own tiny bond wires.

articles.title: NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online
articles.excerpt: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission,…
articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.
